title: Bibliometric analysis of radiology residency theses in Türkiye: publication metrics and trends
question: How often are radiology residency theses in Türkiye published as journal articles, and in which journals?

bottom_line.question: How often are radiology residency theses in Türkiye published as journal articles, and in which journals?
bottom_line.answer: Of 3,136 radiology residency theses, 1,165 (37.1%) were published as journal articles, and 20.8% of all theses appeared in SCIE-indexed journals.

provenance.quote: Out of the 3,136 radiology residency theses, 1,165 (37.1%) were found to have been published as scientific articles in national or international peer-reviewed journals. Among all theses, the publication rate in journals indexed in the SCIE was 20.8% (n = 651).

sections.title: Why Study Radiology Theses
sections.markdown:
In Türkiye, every doctor training to be a radiologist must write an original research thesis before taking the specialty exam. Some European countries have similar rules. Over five decades this rule has produced thousands of theses. The authors asked how many of them ever reach a peer-reviewed journal, and what separates the ones that get published from the ones that stay in the archive.

Their method is **bibliometric analysis**, which means collecting statistics about academic documents: how many were produced, where they were published, how often they were cited, and how those numbers change over time. Theses in several other Turkish medical specialties had already been studied this way. In February 2025, when this work began, nobody had done the same for radiology.

sections.title: How the Study Worked
sections.markdown:
The team pulled radiology residency theses from Türkiye's National Thesis Center, the online database of the Council of Higher Education, with no date limit. They dropped three kinds of records:

- theses with missing data or restricted access
- theses from other specialties that had been filed under radiology by mistake
- anything dated January 2025 or later, because turning a thesis into a paper takes at least six months

That left 3,136 theses written between 1971 and December 2024.

For each thesis they recorded the author's gender, the advisor's gender and academic rank, the institution type (university hospital or training and research hospital), the study design and the year, among other details. Two radiology consultants sorted every thesis into one of 14 topic groups based on the Turkish Society of Radiology's subspecialties. Examples include neuroradiology, breast radiology, interventional radiology, and imaging physics and radiation safety.

Next they looked for each thesis in print. They searched Google, Google Scholar, PubMed, Web of Science, TR Index (a national citation index for Turkish journals) and DergiPark (a Turkish publishing platform), using the author's and advisor's names plus topic keywords. Conference abstracts were excluded, so only full research articles counted. For each match they recorded the journal, the citation count, the first author, and the number of days between finishing the thesis and publishing the article.

Each article was ranked by how its journal was indexed at the time the article appeared. A journal listed in several indexes was placed only in its highest tier:

1. Science Citation Index Expanded (SCIE), the main Web of Science index of established journals
2. Emerging Sources Citation Index (ESCI), a Web of Science index for newer or regional journals
3. Other international indexes
4. TR Index
5. Other national peer-reviewed journals

For SCIE articles they also noted the journal's impact factor quartile for that year. Q1 is the top quarter of journals in a field and Q4 is the bottom quarter.

The main outcome is the **publication rate**, the percentage of theses that became journal articles:

publication rate = 100 x (theses published as articles / all theses)

Citation counts and publication delays were lopsided, with a few very large values, so the authors used tests that don't assume a bell curve. They used chi-squared tests for proportions and Mann–Whitney U and Kruskal–Wallis tests to compare groups. Regression models tested for trends over time. A P value below 0.05 counted as significant.

sections.title: What They Found
sections.markdown:
Most theses came from university hospitals (83.1%). Most advisors were professors (45.8%) or associate professors (33.4%). Thesis numbers rose significantly after 2000 and peaked at 198 in 2010. Neuroradiology was the most common topic (16.0%), followed by abdominal radiology (13.3%) and interventional radiology (12.4%). Imaging physics and radiation safety was the rarest, at 1.6%. Most theses (86.7%) were retrospective, meaning they analyzed existing records and images.

Of the 3,136 theses, 1,165 (37.1%) became journal articles. Of those, 651 (20.8% of all theses) appeared in SCIE journals, which is more than half (55.9%) of the published articles. However, 39.2% of the SCIE articles were in Q3 or Q4 journals, the lower half by impact factor. The most common outlets were Diagnostic and Interventional Radiology (7.0% of articles) and the European Journal of Radiology (4.2%). TR Index journals carried 20.2% of the articles and ESCI journals 11.6%.

The median time from thesis to article was 1,300 days, about three and a half years. The middle half of articles took between 826 and 2,106 days. Most articles were rarely cited. The median was 3 citations, and a few heavily cited papers (up to 416 citations) raised the mean to 14.7.

Over the decades, the odds of a thesis being published rose significantly (P = 0.045) and the time to publication fell significantly (P < 0.001). An earlier study covering 1980 to 2005 found only 6.3% of Turkish radiology theses in SCIE journals. This study found 20.8%.

Several factors made no significant difference:

- Topic. Publication rates ranged from 51.0% (imaging physics and radiation safety) down to 32.6% (breast radiology), but topic had no significant link to publication rate, citations or speed.
- Resident gender, for publication rate and citations. However, female residents took significantly longer to publish.
- Advisor gender, on every measure.
- Institution type, for publication rate and speed. However, articles from universities were cited significantly more.

Advisor rank did matter. Theses supervised by assistant professors, the most junior faculty rank, had the highest publication rate at 43.0%. That was significantly higher than for theses supervised by professors (34.8%, the lowest) or associate professors.

The clearest pattern involved first authorship. Residents were first author on 76.4% of published articles, advisors on 12.9% and other researchers on 10.7%. When the resident was first author, 50.8% of articles went to SCIE journals. That share was 74.7% when the advisor was first author and 69.6% for another researcher. Articles led by advisors or other researchers were also cited more and published faster. On these measures, advisors and other researchers did not differ significantly from each other.

sections.title: What It Means
sections.markdown:
Compared with thesis studies in other Turkish specialties, radiology falls in the upper-middle range. Its publication rate is higher than in anesthesiology, general surgery, family medicine and emergency medicine, among others. It is lower than in thoracic surgery, child and adolescent psychiatry, and endocrinology. The authors note that the studies covered different time periods and used different methods, so these comparisons are rough.

The growth in thesis numbers matches the growth in radiology training posts, which rose from 38 in 2008 to 105 in 2018. Quotas increased sevenfold after 2022, and training lasts five years, so the authors expect more theses soon.

Neuroradiology, abdominal radiology and interventional radiology probably dominate because they have large patient populations and varied imaging methods. Together they also get 15 months of the national training curriculum. The authors are concerned by how few theses cover physics and radiation safety, because earlier studies found gaps in radiation safety knowledge among Turkish radiology staff. Obstetric radiology is also rare, possibly because obstetricians do most obstetric imaging in Türkiye.

The share of articles in lower-quartile journals may partly reflect how many theses were retrospective. Earlier research links prospective and experimental studies to higher-impact journals. Cost also plays a part. Turkish researchers value journal prestige, but high article processing charges push some authors toward lower-impact journals. The authors add that careful retrospective work can still be useful in a data-rich field like radiology. They also note that TR Index and ESCI journals give early-career researchers reasonable places to publish.

The improvement over time may be linked to the Council of Higher Education's promotion rules. These rules give more credit for papers in internationally indexed journals such as SCIE, which gives both advisors and residents a reason to publish.

The assistant professor result goes against the common assumption that senior advisors produce the most papers. The same pattern has been reported in anesthesiology, otorhinolaryngology and plastic surgery. The authors suggest that assistant professors, who are still working toward promotion, put more effort into getting theses published.

The first-author results suggest residents do much of the publishing work themselves. Their articles appear more slowly and in lower-tier journals than those led by more experienced colleagues, who know more about academic writing, choosing a journal and managing submission. The authors take this as a sign that residents need more hands-on mentoring. The slower publication among female residents matches reports from psychiatry and ophthalmology that women face more obstacles in publishing.

sections.title: Limitations and Bottom Line
sections.markdown:
## Limitations

- Articles in small or hard-to-find journals may have been missed, and Scopus was not searched separately.
- Theses were matched to articles by names and content similarity, without direct confirmation, so some matches may be wrong.
- Citation counts are a snapshot in time and undercount recent papers.
- Publication usually takes more than two years, so many 2023 and 2024 theses may not be published yet. This lowers the recent publication rates.
- Only theses held by the National Thesis Center were included.

## Bottom line

About one in three Turkish radiology residency theses becomes a journal article, and about one in five reaches an SCIE journal, though many of those are lower-impact journals. Over the decades, publication has become more common and faster. The factors linked to better outcomes involve people: junior faculty advisors and experienced first authors. The authors call for stronger mentorship, structured training in how to publish, and better research infrastructure. They argue that residency theses should count as research in their own right as well as meeting a graduation requirement.

anchors.sentence: Compared with thesis studies in other Turkish specialties, radiology falls in the upper-middle range.

anchors.quote: Thesis topics were categorized into 14 subgroups based on the subject areas defined with reference to the Education and Scientific Research Groups of the Turkish Society of Radiology (TSR): Neuroradiology, Head and Neck Radiology, Musculoskeletal Radiology, Breast Radiology, Thoracic Radiology, Abdominal Radiology, Genitourinary Radiology, Interventional Radiology, Cardiovascular Radiology, Imaging Physics and Radiation Safety, Obstetric Radiology, Emergency Radiology, Pediatric Radiology, and Other (for theses not falling into the aforementioned 13 groups).

anchors.sentence: The authors are concerned by how few theses cover physics and radiation safety, because earlier studies found gaps in radiation safety knowledge among Turkish radiology staff.
anchors.quote: The low number of theses in the field of imaging physics and radiation safety in Türkiye is concerning, especially given the reported deficiencies in radiation safety knowledge among radiology personnel and the fundamental importance of physics for image quality., This limited representation may be attributed to residents’ tendency to focus on clinically oriented fields and the relatively low level of academic interest in these topics.

anchors.sentence: Obstetric radiology is also rare, possibly because obstetricians do most obstetric imaging in Türkiye.
anchors.quote: The low proportion of theses in obstetric radiology may be attributed to several factors previously described in the literature, including insufficient training duration, limited theoretical content, and a lack of hands-on experience in this field., In addition, obstetric imaging in Türkiye is predominantly performed by obstetricians, which may reduce radiology residents’ exposure to this subspecialty and, consequently, their motivation to pursue thesis work in this area.

anchors.sentence: The share of articles in lower-quartile journals may partly reflect how many theses were retrospective.

anchors.sentence: Cost also plays a part.
Turkish researchers value journal prestige, but high article processing charges push some authors toward lower-impact journals.

anchors.sentence: The authors add that careful retrospective work can still be useful in a data-rich field like radiology.

anchors.sentence: They also note that TR Index and ESCI journals give early-career researchers reasonable places to publish.

anchors.sentence: The improvement over time may be linked to the Council of Higher Education's promotion rules.
anchors.quote: This trend may be associated with the updated academic promotion criteria established by the Council of Higher Education., In particular, the increased academic credit awarded for publications in internationally indexed journals, such as those in the SCIE, has become a motivating factor for both advisors and residency students to publish their theses.

anchors.sentence: Articles in small or hard-to-find journals may have been missed, and Scopus was not searched separately.

anchors.quote: The thesis–article linkage was based on name and content similarity, as direct verification was not feasible, which may have led to occasional mismatches.

anchors.sentence: Citation counts are a snapshot in time and undercount recent papers.
anchors.quote: Due to the time-dependent nature of citation counts, the data—especially for recently published articles—represent only a snapshot and may underestimate long-term citation impact.

anchors.sentence: Publication usually takes more than two years, so many 2023 and 2024 theses may not be published yet.
anchors.quote: In the study by Ozgen et al., which covered the period 1980–2005, the publication rate of radiology theses in SCIE-indexed journals was reported as 6.3%, whereas in our study (covering 1971–2024), this rate increased to 20.8%.

sources.sec-results-3/p3: Out of the 3,136 radiology residency theses, 1,165 (37.1%) were found to have been published as scientific articles in national or international peer-reviewed journals. Among all theses, the publication rate in journals indexed in the SCIE was 20.8% (n = 651). However, when considering only the published articles, more than half (55.9%) appeared in SCIE-indexed journals, and 39.2% of these were published in journals classified under the Q3 and Q4 quartiles ().
sources.sec-methods-1/p1: This retrospective and descriptive study examined the bibliometric characteristics of radiology residency theses in Türkiye, as well as their publication rates in peer-reviewed journals. Theses were retrieved from the online database of the National Thesis Center of the Council of Higher Education of Türkiye. During the search process, “medical residency thesis” was selected as the thesis type, and both “Radiology” and “Radiodiagnostics” were selected separately as the department fields. Records from all available years were included without applying a date restriction. Theses with incomplete data or access restrictions, as well as those belonging to other specialties but erroneously categorized under radiology due to user error, were excluded from the study. Additionally, based on the assumption that the conversion of a thesis into a publication generally requires a minimum of 6 months, theses dated January 2025 and later were excluded. As a result, a total of 3,136 theses were included in the final analysis ().
sources.abstract:
PURPOSE: This study aimed to conduct the first comprehensive bibliometric analysis of radiology residency theses in Türkiye, evaluating publication rates, indexing characteristics, citation performance, and key factors associated with successful thesis-to-publication conversion.

METHODS: This retrospective study included 3,136 radiology residency theses completed between 1971 and December 2024, retrieved from the National Thesis Center. Data were collected on the thesis topic, advisor title, institution type, and study design. Publication status was assessed through searches using author and advisor names and keywords across Google, Google Scholar, PubMed, Web of Science, TR Index, and DergiPark. For published articles, the journal name, indexing category, impact factor quartile, citation count, and time to publication were recorded. Statistical analyses included descriptive statistics, the chi-squared, Mann–Whitney U, and Kruskal–Wallis tests, and regression models (a P value of <0.05 was considered significant).

RESULTS: Most theses were from university hospitals (83.1%) and supervised by professors (45.8%). A total of 1,165 theses (37.1%) were published as journal articles, of which 651 (20.8% of all theses) appeared in Science Citation Index Expanded (SCIE)-indexed journals. Among the SCIE publications, 39.2% were in Q3 or Q4 journals. The most frequent thesis topics were neuroradiology (16.0%) and abdominal radiology (13.3%), whereas imaging physics and radiation safety was least represented (1.6%). Publication rates significantly increased over time (P = 0.045), and time to publication decreased (P < 0.001), with a median of 1,300 days. Theses supervised by assistant professors had the highest publication rate (43.0%, P = 0.013). University-based theses received more citations than those from training and research hospitals (P < 0.001). Residency students were first authors in 76.4% of publications. sources.sec-discussion-4/p7: In our study, 37.1% of radiology residency theses were found to have been published in national or international peer-reviewed journals, and 20.8% of all theses were published in journals indexed in the SCIE. When compared with studies conducted in other medical specialties in Türkiye, these rates are higher than those reported in fields such as anesthesiology, general surgery, public health, family medicine, physical medicine and rehabilitation, and emergency medicine, however, they are lower than those in thoracic surgery, child and adolescent psychiatry, and endocrinology. In neurosurgery, reported publication rates have ranged between 26.8% and 37.9%., Such variation, observed both across different specialties and within the same specialty, may be attributed to differences in study periods, indexing criteria, and overall methodological designs. A similar pattern is also observed across medical specialties in terms of SCIE publication rates ()., , , , , , , , , , , These findings suggest that, in terms of publication output, radiology theses in Türkiye occupy an upper-intermediate position among medical specialties. However, the majority of radiology theses published in SCIE-indexed journals (456 out of 651) appeared in journals ranked in the lower quartiles, specifically Q3 and Q4, in terms of impact factor. The literature emphasizes that experimental and prospective studies not only tend to have higher publication rates but are also more likely to be published in higher-impact and more prestigious journals., In this context, the fact that 86.7% of theses had a retrospective design highlights the need to encourage prospective and methodologically stronger studies. Nevertheless, well-designed retrospective studies can also make significant contributions, particularly in data-rich fields, such as radiology. To improve publication quality, not only the study design but also methodological rigor is a key determinant.
sources.sec-discussion-4/p10: Similarly, Akpinar and Karcaaltincaba reported an increase in Turkish radiology publications after the year 2000 in their study covering the period 1945–2008. This trend may be associated with the updated academic promotion criteria established by the Council of Higher Education., In particular, the increased academic credit awarded for publications in internationally indexed journals, such as those in the SCIE, has become a motivating factor for both advisors and residency students to publish their theses. However, the contribution of alternative indexing platforms should also be acknowledged. In our study, TR Index was the second most common indexing source among published theses, accounting for 20.2% of all publications. Additionally, 11.6% of the publications appeared in journals indexed in the ESCI, a component of the WoS that includes newer or regionally focused journals. These results suggest that both national (TR Index) and secondary international platforms (ESCI) can provide useful publication avenues, particularly for researchers in the early stages of their academic careers or working with limited resources.
sources.sec-results-3/p9: Among the theses that were converted into publications, the rate of publication in SCIE-indexed journals was 50.8% when the residency student was the first author, whereas this rate was higher for publications where the advisor (74.7%) or another researcher (69.6%) was the first author. A statistically significant difference was found between groups when comparing SCIE publication rates according to first authorship status (P < 0.001). Articles with the advisor or another researcher as the first author were significantly more likely to be published in SCIE-indexed journals than those authored by the residency student (P < 0.001 for both comparisons). No significant difference was found between publications with the advisor versus another researcher as first author (P = 0.349).
sources.sec-body/p1: Bibliometrics, defined in 1969, is a method that enables the statistical analysis of academic documents. Such studies reveal research trends and the development of the literature, thereby guiding future investigations. In Türkiye, medical residency students are required to prepare an original thesis in their field of specialization to qualify for the specialty examination. This requirement is explicitly stated in the “Regulation on Medical Specialization Training”. Similar practices also exist in some European countries. The thesis process is a fundamental component of medical education, providing physicians with scientific research skills while contributing to the academic literature. Moreover, residency theses carry significant potential to enrich the medical literature. Thesis data serve as valuable resources for evaluating research trends, knowledge gaps, and academic productivity; their bibliometric analysis is therefore critical for scientific guidance.
sources.sec-methods-1/p4: For each thesis, its status of publication as an original research article was investigated. Conference presentations and abstracts were excluded due to systematic accessibility limitations and lack of alignment with the study’s objectives. Searches were conducted using the names of the thesis author and advisor, along with relevant keywords, across multiple databases and platforms: Google, Google Scholar, PubMed, Web of Science (WoS), and TR Index (a national citation index for Turkish academic journals)., , , , Additionally, DergiPark, an academic publication platform based in Türkiye, was included in the screening process. When a corresponding article was identified, the following data were recorded: article title, name of the journal, country of publication, year of publication, identity of the first author (i.e., whether the thesis author), number of citations (according to Google Scholar and PubMed), and the indexing status. The indexing status was determined based on how the journal was indexed at the time of article publication. Furthermore, the number of days between the thesis completion date and the article publication date was calculated to determine the time to publication.
